certificate.quote: The sequence $\left(f_n\right)_n$ does not converge uniformly, since given $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $N \in \mathbb{Z}_{+}$, for $x=\varepsilon^{1 / N}$ we have $d\left(f_N(x), f(x)\right)=\varepsilon$.
certificate.reason: The equality is unsupported because $f$ is undefined. One must first establish the pointwise limit $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ and $f(1)=1$. Then, for any fixed $\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)$ and every $N$, choosing $n=N$ and $x=\varepsilon_0^{1/N}<1$ gives $|f_N(x)-f(x)|=\varepsilon_0$, which negates uniform convergence. The wording “given ε” can supply such a fixed ε, so the essential gap is the missing definition and justification of $f$.

problem.theorem: Define $f_{n}:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by the equation $f_{n}(x)=x^{n}$. Show that the sequence $\left(f_{n}\right)$ does not converge uniformly.

target_node.claim: Claims nonuniform convergence by choosing, for each positive integer $N$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$, the point $x=\varepsilon^{1/N}$. The calculation requires the unstated pointwise limit $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$; fixing one such $\varepsilon$, for example $1/2$, would then match the negation of uniform convergence.
